clinicalPearls: Also called Gordon syndrome or pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2, caused by variants in WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, or CUL3
The biochemical hallmark is hyperkalaemia with hypertension, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, and a suppressed plasma renin
It is essentially the mirror image of Gitelman syndrome, arising from overactivity rather than loss of the sodium-chloride cotransporter
Hyperkalaemia occurs despite a normal or high glomerular filtration rate, distinguishing it from renal failure
Aldosterone levels are variable but the picture behaves like relative mineralocorticoid resistance for potassium and hydrogen handling
Thiazide diuretics are strikingly effective, correcting both the hypertension and the electrolyte abnormalities by inhibiting the overactive cotransporter
Consider Gordon syndrome in a young hypertensive patient with unexplained hyperkalaemia and normal renal function
reference.pathophysiology: The WNK kinases WNK1 and WNK4, regulated by the KLHL3-CUL3 ubiquitin ligase complex, control the activity of the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Disease-causing variants increase WNK signalling, either directly or by impairing degradation of the kinases, which enhances cotransporter activity and boosts distal sodium chloride reabsorption. The resulting volume expansion produces hypertension and suppresses renin. Because more sodium is reabsorbed electroneutrally in the distal convoluted tubule, less sodium reaches the collecting duct for exchange with potassium and hydrogen, reducing potassium and acid secretion and causing hyperkalaemia with hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. Thiazides reverse the process by blocking the overactive cotransporter.
additionalDifferentials: Drug effects (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes showing hyperkalaemia and hyperchloraemia
Venous blood gas confirming metabolic acidosis
Aldosterone measurement and assessment of the renin-aldosterone axis
Estimated glomerular filtration rate to exclude renal failure as the cause
Sequencing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, and CUL3
redFlags: Accelerated or resistant hypertension causing end-organ damage
Hyperkalaemia worsened by inadvertent use of ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing agents
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent when recognised, because thiazide therapy typically normalises blood pressure and electrolytes; unrecognised disease can lead to complications of chronic hypertension and hyperkalaemia.
pitfalls: Attributing the hyperkalaemia to renal failure despite a normal filtration rate
Prescribing renin-angiotensin blockade, which aggravates the hyperkalaemia
Overlooking the diagnosis in a young patient labelled as essential hypertension
Failing to recognise the dramatic responsiveness to low-dose thiazide
management: Low-dose thiazide diuretic as the strikingly effective disease-specific therapy, correcting both hypertension and the electrolyte disturbance by inhibiting the overactive sodium-chloride cotransporter
Dietary sodium restriction to complement thiazide therapy
Dietary potassium restriction with monitoring to manage the hyperkalaemia
Regular monitoring of blood pressure, serum potassium and acid-base status
Surveillance for and management of hypertensive end-organ complications
Genetic counselling with sequencing of WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3 and CUL3 and cascade family screening
Nephrology referral for diagnosis and ongoing management
